analysis.one_liner: Writes the FTC's "click to cancel" rule into law so ending a subscription is as easy as starting one.
analysis.headline: The bill would make the FTC's click-to-cancel rule permanent law, but it has sat in the Senate Commerce Committee since July 2025 with no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would take the Federal Trade Commission's "negative option" rule — often called "click to cancel" — and write it directly into federal law. That rule requires businesses offering subscriptions or free trials that auto-renew to let customers cancel just as easily as they signed up, typically online in a few clicks. Because a law is harder to repeal or challenge than an agency regulation, codifying it would protect those cancellation rights even if a future administration or court tried to undo the rule. The bill has not moved: it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and no action has been taken since.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers with gym memberships, streaming services, meal kits, and other subscriptions would gain a legal right to cancel online in a few clicks, ending the common practice of requiring phone calls or in-person visits to quit while sign-up takes one click. The FTC would gain permanent statutory authority to enforce the rule.

how_it_helps.text: It gives the FTC's negative option rule the force of statute, so businesses must let consumers cancel recurring subscriptions as easily as they signed up.
Because it is written into law rather than an agency rule, it cannot be undone by a future administration or a court challenge to the regulation alone.

analysis.who_pays: Subscription-based businesses — streaming services, gyms, software companies, and other recurring-revenue firms — would bear the cost of restructuring their cancellation processes and could lose revenue from customers who currently stay subscribed because quitting is difficult.

drawbacks.text: Codifying the rule as it existed on a fixed date (July 7, 2025) locks in one version with no room for the FTC to update it as subscription practices evolve.

Subscription businesses would face new compliance costs to restructure cancellation flows, and some argue the FTC overstepped its authority in issuing the rule — a legal challenge to the rule has kept its future uncertain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and everyday: easier cancellations and penalties for firms that make opting out hard, at modest compliance cost to subscription businesses. The main drawback is that codifying one snapshot of the rule removes the agency's ability to update it as business practices change, and the House has shown no activity, so the bill may not advance at all.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote since July 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Ruben Gallego introduced the bill on July 10, 2025, with Sen. Peter Welch as a cosponsor.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
No further action has been taken: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Subscription businesses that profit from hard-to-cancel recurring charges are better off with the bill stalled, since the underlying FTC rule has faced court challenges.

for.name: Sen. Ruben Gallego
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to codify the FTC's click-to-cancel rule.

for.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and has taken no action on it since July 2025.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors are Democrats, but no committee or floor vote has occurred, so no partisan split is on the record yet.

industries.industry: Subscription-based businesses (streaming, gyms, meal kits, software)
industries.note: They would have to make cancellation as easy as sign-up and could no longer rely on retention tactics like phone-only cancellation. Ordinary consumers save money on subscriptions they meant to end.
Households juggling multiple auto-renewing services would keep money they now lose to subscriptions that are easy to start and hard to stop.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in committee with only two cosponsors in a closely divided Senate. Similar consumer protection measures usually die quietly at this stage unless the committee holds a hearing or leadership prioritizes them; passage before the 119th Congress ends appears unlikely.
